title: The Kitchen of Port Alder
premise: Silas Okonkwo built her career orchestrating other people's perfect days while quietly answering a decade of anonymous letters from someone who signed only 'A.' When A—August Reyes, a ferry-line heir hiding from his family's collapsing empire—moves into the cottage next door in Port Alder, Silas must decide whether the intimacy they built on paper can survive contact with real life, and whether she'll help him fight his corrupt uncle for the ferry company or stay safely invisible. As the last ferry of the season approaches, August's uncle weaponizes Silas's letters to destroy them both, forcing her to claim her voice publicly at the wedding she swore she'd never plan again. In the end, August wins back the company by exposing his uncle, and Silas chooses to stay in Port Alder—not because he asks her to, but because she finally believes she deserves a future tense.
about_author: Yara Lockridge is a former event coordinator who spent six years planning coastal weddings before turning to fiction full-time. She lives in a rented cottage above a shuttered cannery, where she writes about people who inherit more than they asked for.

chapters.title: The Last Train Doesn't Stop Here
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. She arrives in Port Alder to plan one final wedding—the deal that will fund her quiet exit from the industry. Through her meticulous checklists we learn she answers letters from 'A' every month and has for ten years, never asking who he is. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: The Man Who Moved Into the Cottage
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A stranger takes the neighboring cottage: August Reyes, guarded, sea-worn, oddly familiar in his phrasing. He watches her unload wedding supplies with something like recognition. She dismisses it. Beat: first crack in her invisibility; the reader suspects what she won't.

chapters.title: Letters I Never Signed
chapters.summary: August's POV. We learn he has written to Silas since he was nineteen, after a chance encounter on this same dock, hiding behind anonymity because his family's name poisons everything it touches. Now his uncle controls the ferry line, and August has come home to fight or disappear. Beat: longing sharpened by shame.

chapters.title: The Bride Who Wanted Everything
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Her client, Margot Vance, turns out to be engaged to August's cousin—a deliberate alliance between old Port Alder money and the ferry company. Margot demands perfection and drops that the Reyes family will attend. Beat: dread; Silas realizes her two worlds are colliding.

chapters.title: Coffee, No Names
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Silas and August circle each other over shared porch mornings, trading stories with careful omissions. Each recognizes the other's handwriting habits but neither confesses. Beat: tender, comic tension of two people lying by omission about the same truth.

chapters.title: What the Ferry Company Owns
chapters.summary: August's POV. His uncle Edmund pressures him to sign away his inheritance stake, revealing the company's books are rotten—deferred maintenance, bribed inspectors, a near-sinking covered up. August refuses. Beat: the theme of corruption made concrete; stakes widen beyond romance.

chapters.title: The Rehearsal Dinner Disaster
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A caterer cancels; August quietly saves the event with his knowledge of the town's kitchens. Margot notices their chemistry and files it away. Silas nearly tells him about the letters, then retreats. Beat: warmth followed by self-betrayal.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: August's POV. He finds Silas's letter archive accidentally—a box she left in the cottage's shared storage—and reads his own words returned with her replies. He understands why she never signed hers either: she was protecting herself from being known. Beat: devastating tenderness; he decides to let her reveal herself.

chapters.title: Edmund Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Edmund Reyes hires Silas privately: plan the wedding flawlessly and dig up leverage on August, in exchange for funding her exit and erasing her past. She refuses—but doesn't tell August, ashamed she was even asked. Beat: the seed of the third-act rupture.

chapters.title: Storm Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. A storm strands them together; power out, they talk until dawn, closer than ever. August almost says everything. Silas, terrified of being truly seen, deflects with a joke about the last ferry of the season. Beat: peak intimacy built on an unstable foundation.

chapters.title: The Ferry Schedule
chapters.summary: August's POV. He learns the winter ferry line will be suspended—Edmund's cost-cutting that will strand the town and gut its economy. The wedding becomes political: Margot's family are Edmund's investors. August decides to use the wedding gathering to expose him. Beat: romance and rebellion merge.

chapters.title: What Silas Won't Plan
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Margot demands changes that would humiliate August at his own family's table. Silas pushes back and risks losing the fee she needs. For the first time she chooses principle over professionalism. Beat: identity shifting from invisible fixer to person with a spine.

chapters.title: The Almost Confession
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. On the dock at dusk, August begins to tell her about the letters. Silas, panicking that he'll reject her for the deception of silence, cuts him off and says something cruel—that people like him collect people like her as hobbies. Beat: the midpoint wound; both retreat.

chapters.title: Margot's Leverage
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Margot reveals she knows about the letters—Edmund showed her pages stolen from August's cottage—and offers Silas a choice: help discredit August's claims or have her decade of private words read aloud at the wedding. Beat: blackmail; power corrupting the innocent.

chapters.title: The Cottage Is Empty
chapters.summary: August's POV. Discovering his letters missing, August assumes Silas sold him out. He confronts her coldly; she, bound by Margot's threat, can't explain. He packs for the mainland. Beat: darkest hour; the misunderstanding complete.

chapters.title: Reading Someone Else's Mail
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Alone, Silas re-reads ten years of correspondence and finally sees the pattern: A never asked her to be anything but herself. She realizes staying invisible was always the lie. She decides to go to the wedding not as a planner but as a witness. Beat: the turn; reclaiming identity.

chapters.title: The Wedding Day
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The ceremony proceeds under Edmund's smug supervision. August returns anyway, planning to speak. Margot, at the podium, produces the letters to humiliate him. Beat: rising panic; the trap springs early.

chapters.title: Read Them Aloud
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Climax part one: Silas steps forward and takes the letters herself, reading her own replies aloud—claiming every word, every year, every feeling—in front of the town, Margot, and Edmund. The crowd's sympathy shifts. Beat: cathartic courage; love declared in public.

chapters.title: The Ledger
chapters.summary: August's POV. Emboldened, August presents the doctored ferry ledgers he's assembled with the town harbormaster. Edmund's investors defect on the spot; Margot, seeing she was Edmund's pawn all along, withdraws the engagement. Beat: corruption exposed; power overturned.

chapters.title: After the Last Ferry
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The season's final ferry departs without either of them on it. They meet on the empty dock, both having chosen to stay. August asks nothing; Silas stays anyway. Beat: resolution of the central question—presence chosen, not trapped.

chapters.title: Signed, Finally
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Epilogue-adjacent: spring. August runs the ferry line honestly; Silas plans one wedding—her own, small, on the dock. They exchange new letters, signed this time, to be opened in fifty years. Beat: joy earned; the future tense at last.

chapters.title: Port Alder, Population Two More
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Coda: the town settles into winter with its ferry running, Margot rebuilding her life on honest terms, and Silas teaching a letter-writing workshop at the library. Final image: two envelopes in the outgoing mail, addressed to each other, no longer anonymous. Beat: belonging; the story closes on community, not just couplehood.
